title: GC 396 taro (NSIC G 8): Yield, Maturity and Characteristics
metaTitle: GC 396 taro: Yield, Maturity and Characteristics
metaDescription: GC 396 taro is a taro variety. About 8 months to harvest, 11.7 t/ha in trials. See its ratings and traits. Compare it with others.
excerpt: GC 396 is a registered taro variety, also sold or known as NSIC G 8 or NSIC Gb 08. It was registered with the National Seed Industry Council in 2001 as NSIC 2001 Gb 08. It comes from PhilRootcrops, ViSCA (now VSU). It takes about 8 months from planting to harvest, with 11.74 tonnes per hectare on average in the trials.

blocks.text: How long does it take, and how much does it yield?

GC 396 taro takes about 8 months from planting to harvest. That is about the average of the 10 taro varieties with a day count, 8 months. Count the months from planting, and plan the harvest for a dry stretch when you can.

Its average yield of 11.74 t/ha beats the average of its group, 8.82. It sits in the top quarter of its group. Trial yields come from well managed plots, so your own will depend on water, fertilizer, pests and timing.

Once you know the day count, anee.io dates every task from each lot's own planting day, with [the growth stages and weather](/features/growth-stages-and-weather) beside it.
Is it resistant to pests and diseases?

blocks.caption: Reactions in trials, rated under natural field conditions

blocks.text: It showed no weak spot in the ratings on record. Still, a resistant variety can break down when a new strain or pest population comes, so keep scouting.
The pests and diseases that hit taro fields most often: [cutworm](/pests/cutworm). Our [pest finder](/pests) and [disease finder](/diseases) help you name what you see.

Its roots have white tinged with purple flesh and brown skin. Dry matter is 38.27 percent. A higher dry matter cooks mealy and gives processors more flour or starch from each tonne. It is recommended high dry matter content, for food.
What its seller and farm sources say

items: **Fruit:** Brown skin, white flesh tinged purple, pink cortex, high dry matter (about 38 percent).

blocks.text: Why farmers know it: the highest yielding gabi in the NSIC registry list. Check these against what farmers near you have seen, because the same variety can do differently from one town to the next.
Where and when to plant GC 396 taro
It is recommended for anywhere in the country. Gabi grows in wet lowland or on upland beds. Pick a variety for the land you have, and for the corm, the leaves or both.

items.q: Is NSIC G 8 the same as GC 396?
items.a: Yes. NSIC G 8 is another name for GC 396, registered as NSIC 2001 Gb 08. Seed sellers use both, so ask for either one.

items.q: How long does it take to harvest?
items.a: It takes about 8 months from planting to harvest. Then the weather and your care decide the exact day.
The record shows 11.74 tonnes per hectare on average in the trials. Your own yield depends on the soil, water, fertilizer and pests on your farm.
It is recommended for anywhere in the country. Ask your municipal agriculturist how it has done in your town.

items.q: Where can I buy seed of GC 396?
items.a: Ask an accredited seed dealer in your province, the seller named on this page or your municipal agriculturist. Look for the certified seed tag or a sealed pack before you pay.
